source: Di Gioia (2026) Cognitive Friction: decision-theoretic bounded deliberation in tool-using agents
finding: In two simulated worlds, a controller that prices each query (latency, congestion) and halts when net VOI is below cost beat a greedy ask-the-best-tool agent by about 33-36 points. Stopping rules alone recovered at most 4 points. Choosing which test to run, with cost in the score, did most of the work.
numbers: EMDG, N=200 episodes: greedy ReAct viability 56.76, time 114.5; TCA viability 93.03, time 14.5; accuracy 1.00 for both. Entropy-threshold stopping with greedy selection: viability 60.17 (+3.4). Fixed-K=3: 50.92, worse than greedy. NSTG: +33 integrity points.
quote: stopping rules alone recover at most 4 viability points
limits: Synthetic environments built by the author; accuracy saturated at 1.0 by design; single author; no real LLM in the main results.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: a cost-aware ranker plus net-value stop beats a tuned entropy threshold, but in simulation the gain comes from cost-aware selection, not from the stop rule. Test selection and stopping together, not stopping alone.

source: Di Gioia (2026) Cognitive Friction, Appendix D real-LLM instantiation (GPT-4.1)
finding: The net-VOI stop rule was run around GPT-4.1 with sampled-agreement entropy as the belief and one cloned retrieval rollout as the VOI. It retrieved less, but earned less utility than always retrieving. The author calls it illustrative, not a benchmark.
numbers: 25 fictional documents, 60 questions, 5 samples at T=0.7, retrieval cost 1, reward +10/-10. NeverRetrieve U=-10.00 (EM 0.000). AlwaysRetrieve U=+5.33 (EM 0.817, 1.00 retrievals). Net-VOI rule U=+2.20 (EM 0.500, 0.63 retrievals, 72% act, 28% defer). 5 act-without-retrieve cases had zero entropy (all 5 samples identical) and all 5 were wrong.
quote: a known limitation of self-consistency as a belief proxy
limits: Weak keyword retriever on purpose; single model; the proxy lost to the always-test arm at cost 1; N=60.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 and 7: a sampled-agreement VOI proxy underestimates uncertainty when the model is confidently wrong, so the gate skipped checks it needed. A proxy gate needs a floor: never skip a test on agreement alone for high-stakes cases.

source: Fang, Hu, Chang et al. (2026) Inference-Time Budget Control for LLM Search Agents
finding: An action scorer defined as estimated task value per unit of remaining budget (a VOI score, with a budget-dependent penalty) chose between retrieve, decompose and answer. It beat four audited baselines under hard tool-call and token caps in most cells.
numbers: 3 backbones (Qwen3-32B, Qwen3.5-122B, GPT-5.4-Mini), 4 multi-hop QA sets, 4 budgets (1 call/100 tokens up to 3/500). Qwen3-32B: best F1 in 7 of 16 cells, tied in 2; better than AFlow, BATS, Search-o1, BAVT in 14, 10, 16, 15 of 16 cells. Mean wall time -27.2% versus BAVT (20.91s to 15.23s).
quote: The main claim is therefore not that VOI wins every cell
limits: The VOI is an operational heuristic with hand-built structural features and guards, not a payoff-table EVPI. BATS wins at several higher budgets; Qwen3.5-122B is mixed. Authors say 'not a dominance claim'.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 and 2: value-per-remaining-budget scoring helps most at tight budgets (low and lower-mid) and less on the stronger GPT-5.4-Mini. A token-budget VOI gate is most useful when budget is scarce.

source: Fang et al. (2026) Inference-Time Budget Control, Table 1 component ablation
finding: Removing the budget-dependent penalty caused the largest drop in the VOI controller; removing normalisation, structure signals or guards also hurt. The cost term did more than the ranking term.
numbers: Qwen3-32B, upper-mid budget, EM/F1. HotpotQA: BAVT 0.34/0.41, no-penalty 0.35/0.40, full 0.39/0.47. 2Wiki: BAVT 0.40/0.45, full 0.54/0.63. MuSiQue: BAVT 0.26/0.34, full 0.36/0.43. Bamboogle: BAVT 0.33/0.42, full 0.46/0.56.
limits: One backbone, one budget level. Full controller is best on F1 in all four sets, but several single-component removals beat BAVT on some sets.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: the remaining-budget cost term is the part to keep. Net value minus cost, not information alone.

source: Deng, Li, Li, Zhu, Zhao, Guo, Wang (2026) Uncertainty-Aware Clarification in LLM Agents with Information Gain (ICML 2026)
finding: A 1.7B clarifier trained with a reward equal to the Bayesian belief shift toward the true goal raised tau-bench success for five agent backbones, including DeepSeek-R1, while asking about 1.2-1.3 questions on average. More clarification did not keep helping: success peaked at a middle budget.
numbers: Average success across five agents: none 23.6, trained clarifier 27.3 (+3.7), untrained Qwen3-8B clarifier 23.0 (-0.6). DeepSeek-R1 agent average 35.7 to 40.0 (+4.3); Qwen3-8B agent 15.4 to 17.8. General models asked 3.9-5.1 turns; trained 1.3. Budget 0 to moderate: about 15% to over 21%; then plateau or decline. Without the information-gain term: Retail 15.6, Airline 10.0 (Baseline 16.5, 13.3).
quote: success rates peak at intermediate budgets and plateau or decline
limits: Small absolute rates (15-40%); training is on-task; reward uses the ground-truth goal, which an agent at run time lacks; a clarification-enhanced tau-bench variant made by the authors.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 and 8: a reasoning-model agent still gained from a good clarifier, but only a few points. Questions have a peak: set a hard question cap near 1-3 and do not let the count run on.

source: Hartmann, Harvey, Navott et al. (2026) Amortising Bayesian Experimental Design for Sequential Information Gathering in LLMs (ASIG; ICML 2026 workshop)
finding: Training a questioner with an EIG reward more than doubled a 7B model's 20 Questions success, but gave only +4.2 and +1.8 points on the 14B model. The inference-time BED-LLM reimplementation fell below the untrained 14B baseline on Animals.
numbers: Success within 20 questions, %: Qwen2.5-7B Animals base 7.6, ASIG 21.0, BED-LLM 19.2; 7B Plants 6.8, 16.6, 22.8; 14B Animals 35.0, 39.2, 26.4; 14B Plants 11.8, 13.6, 21.0. ASIG costs the same as the base model; BED-LLM is 25x to 36x slower in wall clock.
limits: Workshop paper, non-archival; 5 episodes per setting with large error bars (SE 0.9-4.8); BED-LLM is the authors' reimplementation; Qwen2.5 models, not 2026 reasoning models.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 and 6: the gain from EIG selection shrinks as the base model gets stronger, and expensive per-turn EIG machinery can lose to a plain model. Match the cost of the selector to the gain.

source: Amortizing Sequential Experimental Design in Reasoning LLMs (AR-BED) (2026)
finding: Adding reasoning to the base model did not help it ask better questions: final solve rate fell in every category. A policy trained with a marginalised EIG reward improved, and a controlled test showed two-step lookahead far above one-step.
numbers: Gemma-4-E4B-it policy, GPT-5 as likelihood evaluator. Base with reasoning lowered solve rate in all categories (EIG higher only on Countries). Animals solve rate 43.3% (expected reward) vs 34.0% (realized reward). MediQ dermatology 90.5% to 94.7%; other specialties 84.8% to 90.2%. Cube-NM after five tests: 75.0% two-step vs 30.2% one-step (Qwen3-0.6B). Target prediction at turn 5: 32.7% (K=3), 30.8% (K=2), 29.7% (K=1). Inference per game: BED-LLM 2376 s vs 38.9 s.
quote: inference-time reasoning alone does not improve information gathering
limits: Read through a page fetch that covered the first 100,000 characters; main-figure bars were not readable. Cube-NM is a purpose-built test of non-myopia. The 3-point gap for K=3 vs K=1 is small and no variance was seen.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 and 6: a reasoning-on model is not a better questioner by itself. Lookahead matters hugely where tests only pay off in combination, and only slightly in the natural 20 Questions task.

source: Arnould, Aziz, Kang et al. (2026) CA-BED: Conversation-Aware Bayesian Experimental Design
finding: Propagating EIG through a simulated conversation tree of depth 2 (3 question branches) raised success over direct prompting by 21.8 points on average, at +1.8 turns. It was not clearly better than a tuned UoT setting on 20 Questions.
numbers: DeepSeek-V3.2 Chat, 3 seeds. Detective Cases (100 cases): direct 27.6, UoT 29.0 or 33.0 (two settings), CA-BED 46.0, CA-BED+Answer Planning 38.0. 20 Questions (111 entities): direct 57.7, UoT 60.4 or 90.1, CA-BED 82.9, +Answer Planning 89.2. Mean turns 20Q: direct 9.7, CA-BED 12.8.
limits: Depth fixed at 2: no depth ablation. Token cost of planning not reported ('substantial'). BED-LLM not evaluated. UoT numbers swing 60.4 to 90.1 with two hyper-parameters, so tuning decides who wins. The answerer and the evaluator are LLMs.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: tree lookahead of depth 2 beats one-step direct asking, but no study isolates lookahead depth in natural tasks, and its token price is unreported.

source: MedClarify: information-seeking agent for medical diagnosis (2026)
finding: Choosing the follow-up question by an LLM-simulated expected information gain (plus diversity and consistency terms) beat a naive question-asking arm on three backbones including DeepSeek-R1 and GPT-5.1, with a rule-based stop. Error-reduction claims were stated inconsistently inside the paper.
numbers: 469 cases (NEJM 170, MediQ 129, MedQA 170). Top-1 naive to MedClarify: NEJM 28.0 to 36.1; MediQ 41.2 to 46.1; MedQA 44.3 to 48.4. Backbones on MediQ: GPT-5.1 48.1 to 50.4; DeepSeek-R1-0528 33.3 to 41.1; Llama-3.3-70B 41.2 to 46.1. Questions per case 8.96 vs 9.81. ECE 0.37 to 0.16. Stop at 10 turns, Pmax>0.97 or gap>0.85. Gain over single-shot +26.9 points; over naive about +4 to +8.
limits: Page fetch covered the first 100,000 characters. Subset of cases; LLM simulates both yes and no answers, so the 'information gain' is the model's own forecast. Intro says about 48% error cut, Discussion says 32.3% vs single-shot and 9.1% vs naive.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 and 3: the gain over a plain multi-turn asker is only a few points for strong models (GPT-5.1 +2.3), and larger for a weaker one (R1 +7.8). A useful stop rule is cheap: a posterior cap plus a hard turn cap.

source: Choudhury et al. (2026) BED-LLM, Table 1 (ICLR 2026): 20 Questions with an open target space
finding: Full EIG selection beat prompt-only asking by a wide margin and beat a 'Split' rule (pick the question that halves the sampled hypotheses) by 5 to 30 points. Asking the LLM itself to judge which question is most informative ('implicit maximization') was far worse than computing EIG.
numbers: Success %, 100 targets per set, six models. Animals GPT-4o: prompt-only 45, Split 83, BED-LLM 93, implicit max 70. Celebrities Mistral-Large: 19, 63, 91, 36. Things GPT-4o: 34, 40, 64, 42. Llama-3.1-8B Things: 10, 12, 26, 10. Animals Llama-3.1-8B: 8, 49, 63, 16.
limits: The 'Split' baseline is already strong (and is the same as picking by predictive entropy with deterministic answers), so most of the gain over prompt-only comes from the hypothesis-set machinery, and only part from true EIG. Answerer is an LLM.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 and 5: with a sampled candidate set, even a cheap halving rule recovers most of the gain. Compute the score in code; do not ask the model to pick the best question.

source: Choudhury et al. (2026) BED-LLM: how hypotheses are built when the space is open
finding: The target space is not given. The questioner samples hypotheses from the LLM, rejects those that conflict with past answers, keeps the survivors between turns, asks for diverse batches, and then imposes a uniform weight. Using plain in-context belief tracking instead of that machinery collapsed performance.
numbers: ICL Beliefs ablation, Animals: GPT-4o 25 (vs 93 full), GPT-4o-mini 18 (vs 88), Mistral-Large 53 (vs 95). Things GPT-4o 19 (vs 64). Benefit persisted when questioner and answerer were different models (GPT-4o-mini and Qwen2.5-72B swapped). When the hypothesis set falls to one candidate the agent asks 'Is it X?'.
limits: Targets are well-known entities the LLM can name, so the hypothesis space is open but within the model's prior. No test of what happens when the true answer is never proposed. Uniform weighting is a modelling choice.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: a cheap open-set recipe exists: sample, filter against past evidence, keep survivors, force diversity, weight evenly. The unmeasured risk is the true answer never being in the set.

source: Model Discovery Agent: LLM-assisted Bayesian experiment design (2026)
finding: The LLM only proposes new candidate models when a predictive check shows the pool fits badly; experiments are chosen by a model-disagreement surrogate for EIG over a bounded pool. The paper says the LLM need not propose the right model in one shot.
numbers: ChemBench: 9 canonical models plus up to 12 LLM proposals, pool cap 24; 57 worlds, 3 initial and 22 active experiments. GlucoseBench: 4 starting ODEs, 30 patients, 4 chosen from 48 templates. NeuronBench: 6 neurons, 90 protocols. A wrong model class cost a lot: ODE+BIC 7.41 nMSE vs SDE+SMC 0.38.
limits: Read the abstract, the method and appendices; the main result tables were not in the text I could read (about 178,000 characters unread), so no headline gain is recorded here. 'Open' in name only: the working pool is capped and pruned.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: the practical design is a bounded pool that grows only when a fit check fails, not an unbounded hypothesis list. Model-class errors (not noise) are the main way a wrong set hurts.

source: Exploit More, Explore Smarter for Budget-Constrained Agentic Search (ExTS) (2026)
finding: Treating tree-search expansion as a VOI decision (a virtual child that competes with the best real child) beat standard search at small budgets. Removing the virtual child cut accuracy by 3.2 points.
numbers: HotpotQA prompt optimisation: ExTS 64.89 vs GEPA Pareto 58.55; no virtual child 61.67 (-3.22). LiveCodeBench hard split pass@1: 19.1 vs 18.1 (StandardMCTS) and 17.1 (AB-MCTS-A). DROP workflow F1 90.96 vs CoT 89.28 and AFlow 87.89; cost 15.26 vs 36.70 for CoT. First-play-urgency substitutes 88.95 and 89.34 on DROP.
limits: One model per domain; no direct test of VOI against other expansion scores; some margins are 1 point on single runs. Needs a pilot tree that spends budget.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 and 6: the explore-versus-exploit choice (is one more test worth more than deepening the best branch) is itself a VOI decision, and a simple scoring of it beats fixed rules.

source: CGES: Confidence-Guided Early Stopping for self-consistency (2025)
finding: A Bayesian stopping rule (stop when the top answer's posterior reaches gamma, with a hard budget of 16 samples) cut calls by 58% on average with a 0.4 point accuracy loss. It failed to save much on GPQA where the confidence signal is weak.
numbers: Calls 16.0 to 6.7 on average. Accuracy SC 73.0 vs CGES-DeepConf 72.5. GPQA Diamond: 50.0 vs 47.9 (-2.1). A reward-model variant dropped to 66.7 on AIME24 vs 77.3. gamma swept 0.7 to 0.9999. 10 seeds. Models are 7B (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, Qwen2.5-7B).
limits: Page fetch covered the first 100,000 characters. Small models; no payoff or cost term; the stop is on agreement, not on expected gain.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: a posterior-threshold stop plus a fixed cap of 16 is a workable noisy-test stop. Where the signal is weak, it neither saves nor stays accurate, so a cap is essential.

source: Certified Self-Consistency: statistical guarantees for majority voting (2025)
finding: A sequential 'Martingale Majority Certificate' (e-values, Ville's inequality) stops when the majority answer is certified at error level epsilon, and the guarantee holds at the random stopping time. It saved samples with no accuracy change on MATH-500.
numbers: MATH-500, budget 100, epsilon 0.1: Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B after test-time training, about 61 samples, accuracy 81.0 vs 81.2 at full budget. Pretrained 1.5B: about 86.5 samples, accuracy 36.8 vs 36.6. Qwen2.5-Math-7B pretrained about 75 samples.
limits: Assumes conditionally independent samples given the prompt; only single-turn reasoning sets; free-text answers need canonicalising. Page fetch covered the first 100,000 characters.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: a valid anytime stopping test exists. It is conservative (61 to 86 of 100 samples), so it trades savings for a guaranteed error bound. Our E[N] <= EVPI/c bound is a different (value-based) kind of cap.

source: Saparkhan, Hawasly, Parvez, Raza (2026) Self-Consistency from Only Two Samples: CoT-PoT ensembling
finding: Agreement between two different reasoning modes (a chain of thought and a program) is a stronger stop signal than agreement between same-mode samples. Most tasks stopped after two samples.
numbers: Sampling cut 9.3x; 78.6% of tasks answered with 2 samples (over 90% on some sets); accuracy drop 0.1% versus full sampling; the early-stopping version beat full CoT-only SC by 0.8% accuracy; 5 models including DeepSeek R1.
limits: Needs a task where a program can be run; the drop is an average, not per item.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 and 8: independence matters. Two different kinds of test that agree are worth more than many same-kind repeats, so test diversity should enter the stop rule.

source: Kim, Yang, Min, Jung (2026) Reliability-Aware Adaptive Self-Consistency (ReASC)
finding: Counting only answer frequency stops late; weighting each sample by its own confidence stops earlier at equal accuracy. A single confident sample can end the run.
numbers: Five models (3B to 27B), four datasets. Cost cut up to 70% versus SC (k=16). Example Qwen-2.5-3B GSM8K: SC 89.46 with 18.70 samples; ESC 89.39 with 8.03 (-57.0%); ReASC offline 89.46 with 5.70 (-69.5%).
limits: Confidence calibration is the weak point (authors' own limitation); gains are on small to mid models.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: item-level confidence does predict, at the margin, which items need no further sample, when blended with agreement. It is a gate, not a value estimate.

source: Aggarwal et al. (2023) Adaptive-Consistency and Li et al. (2024) Early-Stopping Self-Consistency (ESC), text re-read
finding: Both stop sampling when a clear majority appears. Adaptive-Consistency uses a Beta/Dirichlet posterior with a 0.95 threshold; ESC stops when a window of 5 samples all agree, with a maximum sampling size L.
numbers: Adaptive-Consistency: up to 7.9x fewer samples, average accuracy drop under 0.1%, 17 datasets, 3 LLMs. ESC sampling reductions: MATH -33.8%, GSM8K -80.1%, StrategyQA -76.8%, CommonsenseQA -78.5%, Coin Flip -84.2%, Last Letters -67.4%, accuracy comparable.
quote: reduces sample budget by up to 7.9 times with an average accuracy drop of less than 0.1%
limits: Savings are small exactly on hard sets (MATH -33.8%): few unanimous windows. Old 2023 models (code-davinci-002, Vicuna-13B).
agent_relevance: Gap 8: agreement stops save most on easy items and least on hard ones, the opposite of where value is. Cap the run by expected value, not by agreement alone.

source: Liu, Fu, Yogatama, Neiswanger (2024) DeLLMa, re-read for utility elicitation and o1 comparison
finding: An explicit decision scaffold (list states, forecast, rank outcomes by elicited utility, maximise expected utility) beat a reasoning model and prompting baselines. LLM-elicited pairwise preferences agreed with human labels 65 to 70% of the time.
numbers: Agriculture / Stocks accuracy: DeLLMa (64 samples) 73.3% / 64.2%; OpenAI o1-preview 33.3% / 35.0%. Agreement with human preference: GPT-4 70.4%, Claude 3 65.3%, Gemini 1.5 69.6%. State-forecast ablation (GPT-4): uniform 58.3, underspecified 55.0, overspecified 56.7, full 60.0. Baselines often below random on large action sets.
limits: Authors annotate preferences themselves (noisy); only two domains; no test of value of information itself.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: LLMs can write a rough payoff table that humans mostly agree with, and the scaffold beat a reasoning model. But 65-70% agreement means payoff tables are noisy, so VOI should be reported with a range.

source: Li, Kim, Wang (2025) QuestBench (Oct 2025 version): reasoning models
finding: Reasoning-tuned models (o1-preview, Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking) still found it hard to say what is missing in Logic-Q and Planning-Q. Chain of thought and few-shot examples gave no significant gains across all models. Models said 'not sure' far less often than they should.
numbers: Planning-Q: Gemini Flash Thinking, Claude 3.5 and GPT-4o said 'not sure' in 1.4%, 4.6% and 0.7% of zero-shot cases when the true rate was 41.8%. Planning-Q models were at most 5% above a random baseline. GSME-Q and GSM-Q were near saturation (GPT-4o on the full sets: 99.39% and 84.05%). Gemini 2.5 Pro appears only in qualitative traces.
limits: No Gemini 2.5, o3 or later model was scored; the clean accuracy table did not extract, so per-model accuracy is not recorded. Claims about 2026 reasoning models stay open.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: 'knowing that you do not know' was not fixed by reasoning models up to o1-preview. The scaffold must detect missing information in code or by forced checklist, not trust the model to say so.

source: Dong et al. (2026) Value of Information: human-agent communication, Appendix A case study
finding: One instance shows the VOI rule stopping early in a low-stake game and asking longer in a high-stake one, where a fixed confidence threshold cannot change. In the high-stake instance the VOI agent still ended with a wrong diagnosis.
numbers: Mixed 20 Questions, communication cost c=0.05, reward 1 (animal) versus 10 (diagnosis); compared with no-ask, fixed-round and confidence threshold 0.90. A single run per task.
limits: Illustration, not a statistic. The main-text numbers (18 of 20 conditions, up to 1.36) were checked earlier; this anecdote adds the stake mechanism only.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: stake-sensitivity is the clear structural advantage of a payoff gate over a confidence threshold. It still needs a reliable payoff scale (reward 1 vs 10 was set by the experimenter).

source: Nelson, McKenzie, Cottrell, Sejnowski (2010) Experience matters: information acquisition optimizes probability gain
finding: Three experiments, with test environments built by computer optimisation so the four theories (information gain, KL distance, probability gain, impact) make different predictions. Probability gain explained human search best after experience-based learning. Verbal summary statistics gave a different pattern, and individual preferences in the two formats were unrelated.
numbers: Chi-square tests of within-subject consistency between experience-based and summary-statistics tasks: all four comparisons nonsignificant. Probability gain better than information gain, impact, and the probability-of-certainty heuristic in Experiment 1; preference robust in Experiment 3.
limits: Human classification tasks with few features, not LLMs. Page text read; per-condition counts not extracted. No LLM study comparing these measures was found.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: probability gain is closest to EVPI-type error reduction, and humans use it. For a closed-form decision with a 0-1 payoff, expected error reduction is the same as the payoff gain, so use it when payoffs are accuracy.

source: Zhang, Xu, Chen (2026) How Do Agent Harnesses Create Value? Planning information and release control
finding: A read-only verifier that checks the final answer rejected most invalid episodes at tiny cost. Which part of a harness was worth more depended on the loss assigned to a wrong acceptance.
numbers: tau2-bench: 265 matched cells; prewritten plans +7.17 points oracle success (90% bootstrap interval 1.15 to 13.36). Verifier rejects 61% of oracle-invalid Retail episodes and withholds 17% of correct ones, under one cent extra per episode. At high liability the standalone verifier captures nearly all the false-pass benefit of the full stack.
limits: Read abstract and layout only (PDF text partly extracted). Retail plus a small Airline pilot; cost figures are per episode.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: the value of a check is set by the loss from a wrong answer. Gate verification by stake, and use a cheap read-only verifier before expensive extra reasoning.

source: Chhikara (2026) Evaluating Confidence-Gated Retrieval with Matched Trajectory Replay, abstract re-read
finding: Calibrating confidence changes which answers are committed but not whether another retrieval will help. The author says retrieval needs its own value-of-information or utility estimate. A map fitted before retrieval stayed calibrated at depths one and two but was worse than raw confidence at depth three on all three models.
numbers: Mistral Small 4, GPT-OSS-120B, Qwen3-235B; HotpotQA and MuSiQue. Accuracy among committed answers up by as much as 41 points at the same threshold, with lower coverage; overall accuracy +15 and -17 depending on setting.
quote: it does not estimate the expected benefit of another retrieval
limits: One author; replay of saved states; abstract and introduction read in this pass, results tables only partly.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: confidence tells how likely the current answer is right, not how much one more test would add. Do not use confidence alone as the test gate.

source: Wikipedia 'Value of information' and 'Expected value of perfect information' (read 2026-10-27); Howard (1966) not opened
finding: The pages state that VOI is never negative because the decision maker can ignore information, that the VOI of two evidence variables is not additive, and that for risk-averse or risk-seeking decision makers a simple calculation can be wrong and iterative calculation is needed. EVPI is the upper bound on any information activity. The pages do not discuss Howard's proofs.
numbers: Howard (1966) is cited as IEEE Trans. Systems Science and Cybernetics 2(1): 22-26 (five pages). Two-choice, two-outcome case: EVPI cannot exceed half the maximum reward difference. No delta property or negative-value case is described.
quote: The VoI of observing two new evidence variables is not additive.
limits: Secondary sources only. IEEE page returned empty; Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex were rate-limited. Raiffa-Schlaifer (1961) and Howard (1966) remain unopened, so the risk-averse claims are second-hand.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: for an agent whose payoff is accuracy (risk neutral), the textbook formulas hold. Treat risk-averse breakdown as a documented caveat, not as a tested result.
